svg.title: Four counter-intuitive truths about Layer 2 design, each with what it really means and the design action it forces
svg.desc: Four rows. Layer 2 has no concept of a destination, because forwarding is a lookup or a flood and frames carry no TTL, so a loop never expires by itself. STP is a patch rather than a design, so every generation removed blocked ports rather than tuning them. Failures are silent, arriving as slow or flaky rather than as an alarm. Redundancy is not reliability unless the failure domains are independent, so the review question is about cabinets, conduits, line cards and carrier points of presence. A note at the bottom gives the test: ports still sitting in blocking or alternate state are the backlog.
svg.text: Four truths that make Layer 2 design different from everything you learned about routing
Each one removes a habit that works perfectly well one layer up
THE TRUTH
WHAT IT ACTUALLY MEANS
WHAT TO DO ABOUT IT
No concept of a destination
no TTL, no error, no route table
a frame is switched or flooded, nothing else
Forwarding is lookup or flood: a known MAC is switched,
an unknown one is flooded. Flooding is normal behaviour,
not an error — so a loop never expires by itself.
Ethernet has no TTL to kill the copy.
Ask which links STP is cutting out
of service. That is the price of
loop-freedom, paid in bandwidth.
STP is a patch, not a design
the goal is to leave it nothing to do
tuning it well is not the achievement
Every generation removed blocked ports rather than tuning
them: RSTP, then clustering, then routed access. Blocking
is the thing to delete, not the thing to optimise.
A better timer is still a timer.
For every feature you add, name
the blocked port or the timer it
removes. If neither, drop it.
Failures are silent
it does not error, it slows down
"it was fine, then it was not"
Symptoms arrive as slow, flaky, "works after a refresh",
or "some machines cannot reach some others". No log line
ever says loop. A MAC flap is the only witness.
Acceptance cannot be "it pings".
Write failure scenarios as tests:
pull this link, expect this path,
within this many seconds.
Redundancy is not reliability
unless the failure domains differ
two boxes can be one single point
Two devices in one cabinet, two links in one conduit, two
uplinks on one line card, two circuits in one carrier POP.
Count failure domains, not boxes on the diagram.
Cases 2 and 5 are exactly this mistake.
Every review asks one question:
are these two failure domains
independent? If not sure, the
availability figure is fiction.
The test that needs no meeting: count the ports currently sitting in BLK or ALTN. That number is paid-for bandwidth earning nothing.
It is also the honest measure of how far the design has travelled — every generation in this chapter exists to push it towards zero.
If the count is zero, the rest of this chapter is about protecting that state. If it is not, the rest of this chapter is about earning it.
